claims.text: The as-processed high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
High mechanical loading makes the nominally single-phase structure locally unstable.
Stress-assisted local chemical ordering or nanoscale phase segregation occurs under high mechanical loading.
The ordered or segregated regions form brittle zones.
These brittle zones reduce overall toughness and promote brittle fracture.
The controlled comparison uses identical specimens tested under high strain rate or high stress intensity versus less aggressive low-strain-rate loading.
Localized deformation is pronounced during high-strain-rate dynamic loading at room-to-moderately-elevated temperatures.
Nanoscale segregation or chemical ordering preferentially develops at stress concentrations such as grain boundaries or heavily deformed grains.
Rapid, high-energy loading enables localized atomic diffusion or reordering.
Localized diffusion or reordering produces brittle precipitates or ordered domains.
Brittle precipitates or ordered domains hinder dislocation motion.
Hindered dislocation motion promotes crack initiation and propagation.
High-strain-rate specimens will exhibit more local chemical ordering or nanoscale phase segregation than low-strain-rate specimens.
High-strain-rate loading will reduce fracture toughness relative to the low-strain-rate baseline.
High-strain-rate loading will reduce ductility relative to the low-strain-rate baseline.
Fractography of high-strain-rate specimens will show features of brittle fracture.
The proposed effect occurs only after strain rate and local stress exceed a threshold at which atomic mobility is sufficient to trigger local ordering.
The proposed mechanism is applicable to transient high-loading service such as aerospace or automotive impact scenarios.
The threshold and extent of segregation depend on alloy composition and processing history.
The stress-induced-segregation explanation would be falsified if high- and low-rate specimens show neither a significant ordering or precipitation difference nor a significant toughness difference.
